title: Generics
subtitle: Type parameters, constraints, keyof, inference, erasure

cards.meaning: They parameterize types the way functions parameterize values. You write one implementation; each call site keeps specific type information instead of collapsing to any or duplicating overloads.

cards.front: Generics vs any vs overloads — why generics exist?
cards.meaning: Without generics you either use any and lose safety downstream, or copy-paste/overload per type, which does not scale. Generics keep one implementation and preserve the relationship (element type in ⇒ same type out) per call. Using any “to make it compile” drops the call-site relationship generics exist to preserve.

cards.front: What does firstElement<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined preserve?
cards.meaning: T is inferred from the argument: [1, 2, 3] gives number | undefined; ['a', 'b'] gives string | undefined. The function is shared; the input–output element relationship is preserved per call.

cards.front: How is T inferred, and when do you pass fn<User>(…)?
cards.meaning: Inference usually comes from arguments. identity(1) infers T; identity<string>('a') passes T explicitly. Pass explicit type arguments when inference fails: no arguments to infer from, conflicting inferences, or too-wide contextual types. Do not force <T> everywhere.

cards.front: Why would a generic have two type parameters?
cards.meaning: To keep two independent relationships. mapPair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B] preserves each argument’s type in the tuple instead of collapsing both to one T or any.
cards.example: function mapPair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B] { return [a, b]; }

cards.front: What is ApiResponse<T> — a factory or a value?
cards.meaning: A generic type alias is a factory for concrete types, not a runtime value. Instantiating ApiResponse<User> fixes data: User and status: number. Same idea for classes: class Box<T> { constructor(public value: T) {} } — each instance carries a concrete T.

cards.front: What does T extends { name: string } do?
cards.meaning: It limits what T may be so you can use known properties. x.name is allowed because the constraint guarantees name: string. Without that extends, x.name is an error. Prefer the minimal constraint that unlocks those properties — over-constraining breaks inference; T extends any is pointless.
cards.example: function label<T extends { name: string }>(x: T): string { return x.name; }

cards.front: T extends Foo vs annotating the param as Foo — difference?
cards.meaning: T extends Foo means T must be assignable to Foo and can be richer. Returning T keeps the full caller type. Annotating the param as Foo alone would widen and drop extra properties.
cards.example: function withName<T extends { name: string }>(x: T): T { return x; }

cards.front: What does getProp<T, K extends keyof T>(obj, key: K): T[K] buy you?
cards.meaning: keyof T is the union of property names; K extends keyof T allows only those names; T[K] is the type of that property. Keys are checked and the return type is exact — typos fail at compile time, unlike (obj: any, key: string): any.

cards.front: What does type Page<T = unknown> mean when you write Page?
cards.meaning: Default type parameters supply a type when callers omit the argument. Page alone is Page<unknown>; Page<User> is UserPage. Needed when there is nothing to infer from (e.g. createSet<T = string>(): Set<T>).

cards.front: Can you instanceof T, new T(), or inspect T at runtime?
cards.meaning: No. Generics are erased — T is not a value. You cannot new T(), instanceof T, or inspect T at runtime. return {} as T in make<T>(): T is a smell: there is no runtime T to construct or check.

cards.front: How do you construct a generic T at runtime?
cards.meaning: Pass a runtime constructor: factory<T>(Ctor: new () => T): T { return new Ctor(); }. The value Ctor exists at runtime; the type parameter T does not.
cards.example: function factory<T>(Ctor: new () => T): T { return new Ctor(); }

cards.front: Why is useAsync generic, and how is state modeled?
cards.meaning: Success state carries data: T inferred from () => Promise<T>, so on success state.data is User after fetchUser. State is a discriminated union: idle | loading | { status: 'success'; data: T } | { status: 'error'; error: unknown }. T only exists on success; error is unknown until narrowed.
cards.example: useAsync(() => fetchUser(id)); // T inferred from Promise<User>

cards.front: How does inference work on List<T> with renderItem?
cards.meaning: T flows from items: T[] to renderItem: (item: T) => React.ReactNode. Write function List<T>(props: ListProps<T>) — React.FC<Props<T>> is awkward for generic components.
cards.example: function List<T>({ items, renderItem }: ListProps<T>) { return <>{items.map(renderItem)}</>; }

cards.front: What is Repository<T, ID> in Nest / TypeORM style?
cards.meaning: One abstraction, many entities: UserRepository implements Repository<User, string> with typed findById and save. Same pattern as TypeORM-style Repository<Entity> — typed IDs and returns without duplicating the interface per entity.

cards.front: Can Nest inject an open generic T?
cards.meaning: No. Runtime DI still needs concrete classes or tokens. Generics do not exist at runtime for Nest to inject “T”.
